<pasted_content id="26b7">
I got an idea for this project at the last minute. I thought about my dad recently complaining about how high the electric bill was. Most of us know the feeling, the impending doom of being the culprit since you are the 'computer person'. I considered that annoyance. (We'll see about that, Dad!) I set out on a mission to prove that I was not a sole contributor to the high electric bills. So I built this app for my dad, so that he would have a resource to understand his electric bill. But this story - and app build - goes much deeper than just a re-invented utility app UI. We are integrating local government data to compare amongst the neighbors, pulling in actual usage data from the electric company, and pairing it with the solar panel technology so we can get a real birds-eye view of what in the heck is happening. I'll be honest, it turned into chaos.

So in the app provide my the solar tech company, they give you a dashboard of your site, panels, production, and a nice grid-view that is supposed to mirror the situation that is happening on your roof. Everything was all fun and games connecting and api here, pulling in a spreadsheet there. The solar tech company even had a free developer portal to use the api. That was fun and exciting to discover. With dad's approval I integrated with no problem. Then I started to dig deeper than anticipated. I learned that there was an optional consumption meter our solar panels could of had, but that was never installed. I learned that there are also devices you can install on your circuit breaker to read what circuit (or room, like my brothers... cough cough) is using what amount of power at any given time. Something cool to maybe have in the future. 

As I pulled in my information from the solar tech company's app, I noticed that two of the microinverters were bad. This was something we already knew. But what was alarming was when my app started alerting me that some random solar panels were underperforming. I was shocked, noting that an additional 4 panels were reporting between 11% - 30% of their regular generation. They were random, not localized to one area. Confused, I stepped outside to see if a squirrel had built a house or something. Nope, nothing strange, just neatly positioned solar panels on my roof... wait. They are going up the roof in a vertical orientation? That's not what they look like on my grid. I double checked. Panicked and confused I went in and out of my house several times, standing on chairs, taking pictures, and showing my dad. Dad! They are not horizontal! 

It took some convincing because it was a difficult angle but I think I finally proved the orientation. Why does this matter? Because in the application I was making - and in the original tech company's official app, they are oriented as horizontal. So, the orientation was a bit off, so what? Well, I also noticed that there was two long rows and then a short row in the app. what was actually on the roof was long-short-long. This definiatly does not match. An actual, bonified, descrepeniy. 

Allow me to explain further.

Somewhere between 2 and 3 years ago we had some storms rip through the neighborhood. Damage was caused to our roof. Fortunatly for us, insurance covered everything. But in order to fix the roof you have to take down the solar panels. We had repairs done to the solar panels while they were down and the roof was being redone. When the work was done the solar panels were reinstalled and everything was fine. This was an 18 month process, since insurance policies drag things out. Shortly after this was completed, the two microinverters stopped responding, so that has been like that for a while. 

But I couldn't figure out why some random panels were underperforming. I hypothesized: "We cut down the trees closest the house so it can't be the squirrels again, we did have wildfire smoke and a dust storm, and paired with bird poop who knows what the story is up there." Things clicked when I remembered that the work was done to the roof and the orientation and placement wasn't lining up. Whoever installed the solar panels must have forgot to rebuild the area, and panels are reporting being in places they are not. To further justify my idea, I went outside to verify that shade from a tree was landing on some of the panels. This was confirmed, however, the panels that were being covered were not the ones that were performing poorly according to the diagram on the tech company's app. All completly wrong and off. 

By current blocker is that I need to call the company and ask why all the solar panels are improperly oriented and placed randomly. This could cost the consumer depending on what technician comes to the house to do the "fixing". If I show the technician that the second panel in the first row is the one with the issue, and he fixes it, stating "We will see it working tomorrow" or whatever, and it in fact is not fixed, how can I prove anything? This could be a big expense, depending on many factors. I need to be certain which panel needs fixing before I start directing people. Telling people "It's that one!" when its actually the one next to it could lead to alot of upset people and money gone - making all of this nearly pointless. So then. I wait for that. 

In any case, I have been setting up my app to work in unison with home assist, and I will be installing smart plugs and sensors to get a more accurate picture of what the hosue is doing, giving my dad a better understanding of energy being used, by whom, and give him ideas about what might need optimization. Also in my defense, I noted that the bill went up after the utility price increased 12% for all residents. Thats a steep step! paired with microinverters in question and a full house, this sheds a bit more light on the situation. I will however be contacting our solar panel company and having a serious word.
</pasted_content id="26b7">

content.text:
This is a strong story. The voice is natural, the funny lines land ("We'll see about that, Dad!", the brother's room), and the panel-map mystery has a real payoff. Writing quality is weighted most heavily, so that's a good place to start from. I compared it with the rules and your code. Here's what needs work, most important first.

**Will hurt you with the judges**

1. **Open-source AI isn't mentioned anywhere.** The rules say it must be at the core, and the post has to explain "why open matters." Right now neither the code nor the post has any. This is the one gap that could disqualify the entry. You can only write about it honestly once something exists. A small local model, such as Gemma running in Ollama, could turn the dashboard's problem list and bill numbers into a plain-English summary for your dad. Then the reasons open matters are easy to write: the household's energy data and location stay on your machine, and it costs nothing to run.
2. **The post never says what the app does.** Judges need a clear list. From the code, it has:
   - live Enphase production
   - problem detection (dead microinverters, underperforming panels)
   - history charts against PVWatts expected production
   - your ComEd bill and usage imported
   - a ranked list of what's using power, from Home Assistant
3. **"Compare amongst the neighbors" doesn't match the code.** PVWatts (from NREL, a federal lab) estimates what *your own* system should produce. It doesn't compare you to neighbors. I'd describe it as government data showing what the roof *should* be producing. That still makes your underperformance point.
4. **Entire isn't mentioned.** To win that category, explain how you used it in a meaningful way: what it recorded, what you got from it, and ideally a link.
5. **Required parts are missing:** a demo (screenshots or a video), a link to the code, and the `#hf26challenge` tag. Use the template from the announcement post as your headings.

**Easy wins**

- **Your dad's reaction** earns bonus points, and you already have a great moment with "Dad! They are not horizontal!" End with what he said about the app itself.
- **The 12% rate increase** is the punchline of your "it's not my fault" setup, but it's buried in the last paragraph. Move it up or give it a moment of its own.
- **Cut down the insurance and roof-repair paragraph.** The 18-month timeline slows things down right when the mystery should be speeding up.

**Typos and wording**

- "could of had" → "could have had"
- "definiatly" → "definitely"
- "bonified descrepeniy" → "bona fide discrepancy"
- "Fortunatly" → "Fortunately"
- "completly" → "completely"
- "hosue" → "house"
- "alot" → "a lot"
- "By current blocker" → "My current blocker"
- "two long rows and then a short row" ✓, but "there was two" → "there were two"
- "So in the app provide my the solar tech company" is garbled; maybe "In the app my solar company provides…"

You have about 5 hours, so here's the order I'd go in:

1. Add a minimal local-model feature to the app, about an hour.
2. Finish Entire.
3. I restructure your post into the template, keeping your voice, and save it to DEV as an unpublished draft for you to review.

Want me to start on the local AI feature? Do you already have Ollama or another local model runner installed?

# Solar dashboard

Private dashboard for the home Enphase system: https://solar-dashboard-coral.vercel.app

```
Home PC ── collector/collector.mjs (every 60 s)
   ├─ IQ Gateway (192.168.1.166, local API, owner token)
   └─ APC UPS (not yet — needs APC USB cable 940-0127)
        │ POST /api/ingest  (Bearer INGEST_SECRET)
        ▼
Vercel (Next.js 16) ── Upstash Redis ── dashboard page (DASHBOARD_PASSWORD)
        ▲
        └─ /api/cron/daily (Vercel Cron, 11:00 UTC) → Enphase cloud API v4
           summary + daily history, ~3 calls/day of the free 1,000/month
```

## Collector

Runs from the Windows scheduled task **Solar Dashboard Collector** (starts at logon, hidden,
logs to `collector/collector.log`).

```sh
node collector/collector.mjs --once --print   # one reading, printed and pushed
node collector/collector.mjs --probe          # dump raw gateway JSON to collector/probe/
```

Config is `collector/.env` (template: `collector/.env.example`). The gateway token expires
yearly — the dashboard's Problems list warns 30 days ahead. Renew at
https://entrez.enphaseenergy.com using the **homeowner** login (not the developer account).

## Vercel environment variables

| Name | What |
|---|---|
| `KV_REST_API_URL`, `KV_REST_API_TOKEN` | Added by the Upstash integration |
| `INGEST_SECRET` | Shared with `collector/.env` |
| `CRON_SECRET` | Sent by Vercel Cron to `/api/cron/daily` |
| `DASHBOARD_PASSWORD` | Login for the dashboard |
| `ENPHASE_API_KEY`, `ENPHASE_CLIENT_ID`, `ENPHASE_CLIENT_SECRET` | Developer portal app |
| `ENPHASE_SYSTEM_ID` | Optional; looked up automatically after connecting |
| `HOME_TIMEZONE` | `America/Chicago` — when "today" starts |

After deploying, open the dashboard and click **Connect Enphase** once to authorize the cloud API.

## Known hardware gaps

- Consumption meter is disabled on the gateway → no home-use / grid data until CTs are installed or enabled.
- Two microinverters (202015011110, 202101033131) have stopped reporting — warranty claim with Enphase.

## ComEd billing data

Download the **billing** CSV from ComEd (Green Button → Download My Data), then:

```sh
node --env-file=.env.local scripts/import-comed.mjs path/to/billing.csv
```

Only the billing rows (dates, net kWh, cost) are stored, in Redis key `comed:billing`; the
name/address/account header is ignored. Re-run with newer downloads — periods merge by start date.
Home use per period = ComEd net kWh + solar produced.

## Where the power goes (per device / room)

## Collector

Runs from the Windows scheduled task **Solar Dashboard Collector** (starts at logon, hidden,

```sh
node collector/collector.mjs --probe          # dump raw gateway JSON to collector/probe/
```

Config is `collector/.env` (template: `collector/.env.example`). The gateway token expires
yearly — the dashboard's Problems list warns 30 days ahead. Renew at
https://entrez.enphaseenergy.com using the **homeowner** login (not the developer account).

content.thinking: Found the bug: microinverters go quiet nightly since they're solar-powered, but the current `isSilent` check wrongly flags all 23 as dead after dark. I'll fix it to only flag a unit as dead after 24 hours of silence—your two genuinely dead ones (810 and 74 days silent) will still trigger correctly.

content.text:
The local AI feature is built, and I tested it with your real data. Nothing is committed or deployed yet.

**What it does:** Every 6 hours, your collector gets a small set of facts from the dashboard: today's and this month's solar compared with what's expected, the latest bill compared with last year, and the problem list. Gemma 3 4B, running in Ollama on your PC, turns those into a short plain-English note for your dad. A **"Dad's briefing"** card near the top of the dashboard shows it, labeled as written by `gemma3:4b` running locally on the home PC. You can switch models by changing one line, `OLLAMA_MODEL` in `collector/.env`. I've already added that line, set to `gemma3:4b`.

Here's what Gemma wrote tonight from your real data, in 21 seconds:

> Overall, your solar panels produced a good amount of electricity this month.
> - The microinverters 202015011110 and 202101033131 are not reporting. You need to contact Enphase support…
> - Your electric bill is $270.48, which is much higher than last year's $46.12…
> - Solar panels covered 41% of your electricity use.

**I also fixed an existing bug.** After sunset the dashboard was showing "0 of 23 panels working" with 21 false critical alerts, because every microinverter goes quiet at night. Now a microinverter only counts as dead if it hasn't reported in 24 hours. It correctly shows 21 of 23, and your two real dead units are still flagged.

The type checker and linter both pass. I confirmed the card shows up on a local dev server.

**To make it live, you need to:**
1. **Commit and push to deploy.** Want me to commit, then push to `master`? That deploys to your production Vercel site.
2. **Restart the "Solar Dashboard Collector" scheduled task** after the deploy, so it picks up the new code.

**For your post, this gives you real answers to "why open matters":**
- Your family's bills, usage, and location stay on your own PC instead of going to an AI company.
- It costs $0 to run every few hours.
- You can switch to a different model by changing one line.
- Gemma's plain-English summary is what makes the dashboard usable for your dad, which also fits the theme.

The deadline is still about 4½ hours away. Next, I can help finish Entire, or start restructuring your write-up into the challenge template. Which do you want first?

=== search
entire search — Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using semantic and keyword matching
Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using hybrid search (semantic + keyword),
powered by the Entire search service.

Requires authentication via 'entire login' (GitHub device flow).

By default, results are scoped to the current repository. Use --all-repos to
search across all accessible repos.

Run without arguments to open an interactive search. Results are
displayed in an interactive table. Use --json for machine-readable output,
and add --compact for a trimmed per-result shape suited to agents (implies
--json): id, type, repo, branch, author, date, files touched, score, match
snippet, and a truncated title instead of the full prompt (repo hits add
description and checkpoint count). Fetch full detail
for a single result with 'entire checkpoint explain <id>', or add --full to
that command to pull the checkpoint's entire session transcript. For a
checkpoint hit from another repo, add --repo gh/<owner>/<repo> for a GitHub
mirror or --repo et/<project>/<repo> for an Entire-native repo. The forge
prefix and full checkpoint ID are required; this is unrelated to this
command's --repo filter below.

CLI queries also support inline filters like author:<name>, date:<week|month>,
branch:<name>, repo:<owner/name>, and repo:* to search all accessible repos.

Examples:
entire search "retry backoff" --json
  entire search "retry backoff" --json --compact
  entire search "auth timeout author:alice date:week"
  entire search --code "parseToken"

Current repo: gh/AnnaVi11arrea1/solar-dashboard  (auto-detected from origin; pass --repo only for a DIFFERENT repo)

      --all-repos        Search all accessible repos instead of just the current one
      --author string    Filter by author name
      --branch string    Filter by branch name
      --case-sensitive   Case-sensitive code search (only with --code)
      --code             Search code content across repositories
      --compact          Trimmed JSON output for agents: id, repo, files touched, score, match snippet, and a truncated title instead of the full prompt (implies --json)
      --date string      Filter by time period (week or month)
      --json             Output as JSON
      --limit int        Maximum number of results (per page for checkpoint search, total for --code) (default 10)
      --page int         Page number (1-based) (default 1)
      --repo strings     Filter by repository (gh/owner/repo, et/proj/repo, owner/repo, ULID, or *); repeatable and comma-separated for multiple repos

entire session attach — Attach an existing agent session
Attach an existing agent session that wasn't captured by hooks.

This creates a checkpoint from the session's transcript and links it to the
last commit. Use this when hooks failed to fire or weren't installed when
the session started, or to attach a research session.

If the last commit already has a checkpoint, the session is added to it.
Otherwise a new checkpoint is created.

Use --review to tag the attached session as an agent review. The
first user prompt in the transcript is recorded as the review prompt.
Pass --skills to declare which skills were actually run; omit to
attach a review without a declared skills list.

Works with any registered agent, including external agents enabled via
external_agents in .entire/settings.local.json (that file only, and only
when it is untracked). Run 'entire agent list' to see the full list.

If --agent doesn't locate a transcript, Entire auto-detects the agent from
the transcript and prints the detected agent name.

content.text:
Entire is mostly working: it's turned on, it's hooked into Claude Code, and you're logged in. But two problems would break the searching and "why" explanations you want.

**What's wrong**

1. **Your checkpoints never leave your machine.** `push_sessions` is set to `false` in `.entire/settings.local.json`. The commands you want (`entire search`, plus the web view) read checkpoints from GitHub. Right now your one saved checkpoint exists only locally, so search can't find it.
2. **Most of your sessions aren't connected to commits.** The main build session (Enphase, the problems list, history) is saved properly as part of commit `3146f22`. These ones aren't:
   - the private-repo and Vercel setup session
   - both sessions where you set up Entire itself
   - this session (Gemma and the night-time fix)

   Those commits were made before Entire's commit hook was running, or without it. So their sessions are either temporary or not captured at all, and `entire why` can't explain those lines.

**What I'd do**

1. **Commit the Gemma briefing work now.** Entire's hook is active in this session, so the commit automatically gets this session linked to it.
2. **Attach the sessions that were missed** with `entire session attach`: the Vercel/private-repo one and the two Entire-setup ones. They get linked to that same new commit, so nothing that's already pushed gets rewritten.
3. **Turn on checkpoint pushing** by changing `push_sessions` to `true` in that local settings file.
4. **Push to `master`.** This deploys the Gemma feature to Vercel and uploads all the checkpoints to GitHub.
5. **Generate summaries and test** with `entire checkpoint explain --generate` on each checkpoint. That writes the plain "why it was done" summary. Then I'll test searches like `entire search "panels show dead at night"` and `entire why lib/problems.ts:33`, so you know it works before you rely on it.

**Two things to know before you agree:**
- Pushing checkpoints uploads your session transcripts to your **private** GitHub repo. Your secret scanners and PII redaction run first. If you later want judges to see them, you'd make the repo public or link to Entire's checkpoint pages, and you should look through them before doing that.
- The push deploys the Gemma briefing to your live dashboard. I tested it locally and it passes the type checker and linter.

Should I go ahead with all five steps?

{"Ok":"Hacktoberfest is here, and so is the first of our [**five Hacktoberfest DEV Challenges**](https://dev.to/devteam/hacktoberfest-2026-dev-challenges-five-challenges-one-prompt-a-new-theme-every-week-1e54): a **[Weekend Challenge](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-weekend-2026-10-01)** sized to fit into your weekend.  We've set the timing so that wherever you are in the world, you'll have most of your Saturday and Sunday to build.

> **This year's Hacktoberfest is not about open source pull requests.**  There's no PR count to hit and no repos to hunt for.  Instead, you build a brand-new project with open-source AI at its core, and write about it on DEV.  [Here's everything you need to know about Hacktoberfest 2026.](https://dev.to/mlh/everything-you-need-to-know-about-hacktoberfest-2026-ai-belongs-to-everyone-mdk)

We'll select **one overall winner** and a winner in each of our **16 partner categories**.  See all five challenges and every partner category on the **[HF26 DEV Challenge Hub](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26)**.

Let's get to it!

{% card %}

## Our Prompt: Build for a Friend

**Build something with open-source AI at its core that solves a real problem for a friend or someone you love.**

That can mean running an open-weight model, building on an open-source agent harness or framework, running inference locally, or all three.  Whatever you pick, the open pieces should be what makes your project work.

Pick one real person and build something for them.  It doesn't have to be big.  It has to matter to them.  A few ideas to get you going:

- A meal planner that knows your roommate's allergies
- A patient practice partner for a friend learning a new language
- A tool that turns your grandpa's voice memos into a family recipe book

In your post, tell us **why open innovation matters for what you built**.  Does it run on a laptop with no internet?  Keep someone's data off a server they don't control?  Let you fine-tune, swap models, or change how your agent behaves?  Cost nothing to run?  Tell us where your open-based approach worked better than a closed one.

Bonus points if you actually hand it over and tell us what they said.

{% endcard %}

## Prize Categories

Alongside our overall winner, we have 16 prize categories for projects that use a specific partner's technology.  **You don't need to use any of these to win the overall prize, but if you've been curious about any of this tech, this is a great excuse to give one a try.**  Full descriptions are on the [hub](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26).

**Featured categories:**

- **[Best Use of Render](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-render)**
- **[Best Use of TabPFN](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-tabpfn)**
- **[Best Use of Tinker](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-tinker)**
- **[Best Use of Arduino](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-arduino)**
- **[Best Use of DigitalOcean](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-digitalocean)**
- **[Best Use of Gemma](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-gemma)**

**Partner categories:**

- **[Best Use of Backboard](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-backboard)**
- **[Best Use of ElevenLabs](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-elevenlabs)**
- **[Best Use of Entire](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-entire)**
- **[Best Use of GitHub Copilot](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-github-copilot)**
- **[Best Use of Mastra](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-mastra)**
- **[Best Use of MongoDB Atlas](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-mongodb-atlas)**
- **[Best Use of Sentry Agent Tracing](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-sentry-agent-tracing)**
- **[Best Use of SerpApi](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-serpapi)**
- **[Best Use of Temporal](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-temporal)**
- **[Best Use of Tiger Data](https://dev.to/challenges/hf26#best-use-of-tiger-data)**

> **Pro Tip:** Partner category winners come from a smaller pool of submissions, so your odds are meaningfully higher.

> **Note:** One project can enter every category it genuinely uses, but you can win once per challenge, and we'll aim to celebrate as many different builders as possible across the month.

**Free credits:** several partners are giving participants credits and promo codes, including Tinker, Render, Backboard, and ElevenLabs.  Claim yours at [hacktoberfest.com/my](https://hacktoberfest.com/my).

**A huge thank you to our partners for making these prizes possible!**

## Judging Criteria

This is DEV, so **your write-up matters most**.

- **Writing Quality (weighted most heavily):** Is the post clear and engaging?  Does it explain what you built, who it's for, and why open innovation matters?
- **Relevance to the Prompt and Theme:** Is open-source AI at the core of the project?  Does it fit this challenge's theme?
- **Creativity:** Is it an original idea, or a fresh take on a familiar problem?
- **Technical Execution:** Does it work, and is it well built?
- **Use of Partner Technology (optional):** If you're entering a partner category, does the project use that technology in a meaningful way?

**Show your work.**  We'd love to see how you built it.  Save your agent session with [DevRelay](https://devrelay.com) and embed it in your post, or link to it.  It's optional, but it helps the judges understand your process.

### Prizes

- **Overall winner (1):** $250 USD, a [DEV++](https://dev.to/++) membership, and an exclusive DEV badge
- **Featured category winners (6):** $200 USD and an exclusive DEV badge each
- **Partner category winners (10):** $100 USD and an exclusive DEV badge each

**All participants** with a valid submission will receive a completion badge.

{% card %}

## How To Participate

Publish a post on DEV using the submission template below.  Tell us what you built and who it's for, show us a demo, and explain why open innovation matters for what you built.

Submission Template
{% endcta %}

_Please review our [judging criteria, rules, guidelines, and FAQ page](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-weekend-2026-10-01) before submitting so you understand our participation guidelines and official contest rules, such as eligibility requirements._

{% endcard %}

## Need Help?

- New to Hacktoberfest this year?  Start with [Everything You Need To Know About Hacktoberfest 2026](https://dev.to/mlh/everything-you-need-to-know-about-hacktoberfest-2026-ai-belongs-to-everyone-mdk).
- Come hang out and ask questions in the [MLH Discord](https://discord.com/invite/mlh).
- The [challenge page](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-weekend-2026-10-01) has resources from our partners to help you get started.

## Important Dates

- **Launch:** October 2, 2026, 2:00 AM UTC
- **Submissions due:** October 5, 2026, 6:59 AM UTC
- **Winners announced:** week of October 5

| Timezone | Launch | Submissions Due |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **PDT** | Thu Oct 1, 7:00 PM | Sun Oct 4, 11:59 PM |
| **EDT** | Thu Oct 1, 10:00 PM | Mon Oct 5, 2:59 AM |
| **GMT** | Fri Oct 2, 2:00 AM | Mon Oct 5, 6:59 AM |
| **CEST** | Fri Oct 2, 4:00 AM | Mon Oct 5, 8:59 AM |
| **IST** | Fri Oct 2, 7:30 AM | Mon Oct 5, 12:29 PM |
| **JST** | Fri Oct 2, 11:00 AM | Mon Oct 5, 3:59 PM |
| **AEST** | Fri Oct 2, 12:00 PM | Mon Oct 5, 4:59 PM |

Then [a new challenge launches every Monday in October](https://dev.to/devteam/hacktoberfest-2026-dev-challenges-five-challenges-one-prompt-a-new-theme-every-week-1e54).  Follow [#hf26challenge](https://dev.to/t/hf26challenge) so you don't miss a theme reveal.

Happy Hacktoberfest, and good luck!"}

input.title: My Dad Blamed Me for the Electric Bill, So I Built Him a Solar Dashboard (and Found Panels Where the Map Says They Aren't)
input.description: A solar + electric-bill dashboard for my dad, explained in plain English by Gemma running locally, and the roof mystery it uncovered.
input.body_markdown:
*This is a submission for the [Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-weekend-2026-10-01)*

## What I Built

My dad recently complained about how high the electric bill was. Most of us know the feeling: the impending doom of being the culprit, because you're the "computer person." (We'll see about that, Dad!)

So I set out on a mission to prove I was not the sole contributor to the high electric bill, and I built my dad a resource to actually understand it. It turned into much more than a re-skinned utility app. It pulls together:

- **Live data from our solar panels**, straight from the Enphase gateway on our home network, every minute, down to each individual panel
- **A Problems list** that flags dead microinverters, panels producing less than their neighbors, expiring tokens, and big jumps in home usage
- **Government data on what our roof *should* produce**: PVWatts, a model from the U.S. national renewable energy lab, drawn as markers on the monthly chart so we can see if we're falling short
- **Our actual electric bills** from ComEd, combined with the solar data to work out how much power the house really uses, compared to last year and to the average Illinois home
- **Where the power goes**: per-device and per-room usage from smart plugs in Home Assistant, ranked by what each one costs per month
- **Dad's briefing**: a short, plain-English note at the top of the dashboard, written by **Gemma running locally on our home PC**, that explains all of the above without a single chart

I'll be honest, it turned into chaos.

📸 **[SCREENSHOT: full dashboard]**

### The roof mystery

Everything was fun and games at first, connecting an API here, pulling in a spreadsheet there. Our solar company even has a free developer portal. Then I started digging deeper than I'd planned. I learned there was an optional consumption meter our system could have had, but it was never installed. I learned you can put devices on your circuit breaker to see which circuit (or room, like my brother's... *cough cough*) is using what at any moment.

We already knew two of the microinverters were bad. What alarmed me was when my app started warning that some *random* panels were underperforming: four more, reporting between 11% and 30% of their normal output. They weren't clustered in one area.

Confused, I stepped outside to see if a squirrel had built a house up there. Nope, just neatly positioned solar panels... wait. **They run up the roof vertically.** That's not what they look like on the map. I went in and out of the house several times, standing on chairs, taking pictures, and showing my dad. *Dad! They are not horizontal!*

📸 **[PHOTO: the panels on the roof]** · 📸 **[SCREENSHOT: the panel map in the app]**

It took some convincing from a difficult angle, but I proved it. And it wasn't just the orientation. The official app (and mine, since it uses the same layout) shows two long rows and then a short row. What's actually on the roof is **long, short, long**. A bona fide discrepancy.

Here's why. Two to three years ago, storms ripped through the neighborhood and damaged our roof. Insurance covered it, but to fix a roof you have to take the solar panels down. The whole process took 18 months. When the panels went back up, everything *seemed* fine. Shortly after, the two microinverters stopped responding.

I'd been blaming the underperformers on wildfire smoke, a dust storm, and bird poop. Then it clicked: whoever reinstalled the panels never updated the map. **The system reports panels in places they are not.** To test it, I checked where a tree's shade actually lands. It does cover some panels. Just not the ones the map says are underperforming.

Why does this matter? If I point a technician at "the second panel in the first row" and it's really the one next to it, he "fixes" the wrong panel, says "you'll see it working tomorrow," and I can't prove anything. That could get expensive. Before I start directing people, I need to know exactly which panel is which. That call to the solar company is coming, and it's going to be a serious one.

### So, was it me?

📸 **[SCREENSHOT: Home use & grid card]**

Partly in my defense: ComEd raised prices about 12% for all residents. Add two dead microinverters (plus whatever is going on with the mystery panels) and a full house, and the bill makes a lot more sense. To be fair, the dashboard also says the house really is using more power than last year, which is exactly why the smart plugs are next. Soon we'll know *who*.

**[YOUR DAD'S REACTION: what did he say when he saw it?]**

## Demo

📸 **[SCREENSHOTS / SHORT VIDEO: dashboard, Problems list, panel map, Dad's briefing]**

The live dashboard is password-protected because it shows our home's real data. **[Add a demo login or video here so judges can see it.]**

## Code

{% github AnnaVi11arrea1/solar-dashboard %}

**[Make the repo public before publishing.]**

## How I Built It

```
Home PC ── collector (Node, every 60 s)
   ├─ Enphase IQ Gateway (local API, per-panel data)
   ├─ Home Assistant (smart plug wattage + rooms)
   └─ Ollama + Gemma 3 4B ── Dad's briefing every 6 h
        │
        ▼
Vercel (Next.js 16) ── Upstash Redis ── dashboard
        ▲
        └─ daily cron → Enphase cloud API (history)
```

- **Next.js 16 on Vercel** for the dashboard, with **Upstash Redis** for storage
- **A small Node collector on our home PC** that reads the Enphase gateway on the local network and Home Assistant every minute
- **Enphase's cloud API** (the free developer tier) for years of history, **ComEd's Green Button export** for the bills, and **PVWatts** for expected production

**The open-source AI piece is Gemma 3 4B running in Ollama on that same home PC.** A dashboard full of charts is great for me, but my dad doesn't want charts. He wants to know three things: is the solar working, why is the bill what it is, and does he need to do anything?

Every six hours the collector asks the dashboard for a small set of facts (today's production versus expected, the latest bill versus last year, the Problems list), hands them to Gemma with instructions to explain them like a helpful family member, and posts the result back to the top of the dashboard. It takes about 20 seconds. Here's a real one:

> Overall, your solar panels produced a good amount of electricity this month.
> - The microinverters 202015011110 and 202101033131 are not reporting. You need to contact Enphase support immediately with the serial numbers to get these fixed under warranty.
> - Your electric bill is $270.48, which is much higher than last year's $46.12. This is because your home uses 76 kWh per day, compared to 44 kWh per day last year.
> - Solar panels covered 41% of your electricity use.

📸 **[SCREENSHOT: Dad's briefing card]**

Building the briefing turned up a bug, too. After sunset, the dashboard told us **0 of 23 panels were working**, with 21 critical alerts. Microinverters run on the panels' own power, so after dark every one of them goes quiet, and the gateway's flags can't tell a dead unit from nightfall. If Gemma had read that, it would have told my dad his whole roof had died. Now a panel only counts as dead after a full day with no report.

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

## What I Built

My dad recently complained about how high the electric bill was. Most of us know the feeling: the impending doom of being the culprit, because you're the "computer person." (We'll see about that, Dad!)

- **A Problems list** that flags dead microinverters, panels producing less than their neighbors, expiring tokens, and big jumps in home usage
- **Government data on what our roof *should* produce**: PVWatts, a model from the U.S. national renewable energy lab, drawn as markers on the monthly chart so we can see if we're falling short
- **Our actual electric bills** from ComEd, combined with the solar data to work out how much power the house really uses, compared to last year and to the average Illinois home
- **Where the power goes**: per-device and per-room usage from smart plugs in Home Assistant, ranked by what each one costs per month
- **Dad's briefing**: a short, plain-English note at the top of the dashboard, written by **Gemma running locally on our home PC**, that explains all of the above without a single chart

I'll be honest, it turned into chaos.

📸 **[SCREENSHOT: full dashboard]**

### The roof mystery

Everything was fun and games at first, connecting an API here, pulling in a spreadsheet there. Our solar company even has a free developer portal. Then I started digging deeper than I'd planned. I learned there was an optional consumption meter our system could have had, but it was never installed. I learned you can put devices on your circuit breaker to see which circuit (or room, like my brother's... *cough cough*) is using what at any moment.

We already knew two of the microinverters were bad. What alarmed me was when my app started warning that some *random* panels were underperforming: four more, reporting between 11% and 30% of their normal output. They weren't clustered in one area.

Confused, I stepped outside to see if a squirrel had built a house up there. Nope, just neatly positioned solar panels... wait. **They run up the roof vertically.** That's not what they look like on the map. I went in and out of the house several times, standing on chairs, taking pictures, and showing my dad. *Dad! They are not horizontal!*

It took some convincing from a difficult angle, but I proved it. And it wasn't just the orientation. The official app (and mine, since it uses the same layout) shows two long rows and then a short row. What's actually on the roof is **long, short, long**. A bona fide discrepancy.

Here's why. Two to three years ago, storms ripped through the neighborhood and damaged our roof. Insurance covered it, but to fix a roof you have to take the solar panels down. The whole process took 18 months. When the panels went back up, everything *seemed* fine. Shortly after, the two microinverters stopped responding.

I'd been blaming the underperformers on wildfire smoke, a dust storm, and bird poop. Then it clicked: whoever reinstalled the panels never updated the map. **The system reports panels in places they are not.** To test it, I checked where a tree's shade actually lands. It does cover some panels. Just not the ones the map says are underperforming.

Why does this matter? If I point a technician at "the second panel in the first row" and it's really the one next to it, he "fixes" the wrong panel, says "you'll see it working tomorrow," and I can't prove anything. input.description: A solar + electric-bill dashboard for my dad, explained in plain English by Gemma running locally, and the roof mystery it uncovered.
input.body_markdown:
*This is a submission for the [Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-weekend-2026-10-01)*

## What I Built

My dad recently complained about how high the electric bill was. Most of us know the feeling: the impending doom of being the culprit, because you're the "computer person." (We'll see about that, Dad!)

So I set out on a mission to prove I was not the sole contributor to the high electric bill, and I built my dad a resource to actually understand it. It turned into much more than a re-skinned utility app. It pulls together:

- **Live data from our solar panels**, straight from the Enphase gateway on our home network, every minute, down to each individual panel
- **A Problems list** that flags dead microinverters, panels producing less than their neighbors, expiring tokens, and big jumps in home usage
- **Government data on what our roof *should* produce**: PVWatts, a model from the U.S. national renewable energy lab, drawn as markers on the monthly chart so we can see if we're falling short
- **Our actual electric bills** from ComEd, combined with the solar data to work out how much power the house really uses, compared to last year and to the average Illinois home
- **Where the power goes**: per-device and per-room usage from smart plugs in Home Assistant, ranked by what each one costs per month
- **Dad's briefing**: a short, plain-English note at the top of the dashboard, written by **Gemma running locally on our home PC**, that explains all of the above without a single chart

I'll be honest, it turned into chaos.

📸 **[SCREENSHOT: full dashboard]**

### The roof mystery

Everything was fun and games at first, connecting an API here, pulling in a spreadsheet there. Our solar company even has a free developer portal. Then I started digging deeper than I'd planned. I learned there was an optional consumption meter our system could have had, but it was never installed. I learned you can put devices on your circuit breaker to see which circuit (or room, like my brother's... *cough cough*) is using what at any moment.

We already knew two of the microinverters were bad. What alarmed me was when my app started warning that some *random* panels were underperforming: four more, reporting between 11% and 30% of their normal output. They weren't clustered in one area.

Confused, I stepped outside to see if a squirrel had built a house up there. Nope, just neatly positioned solar panels... wait. **They run up the roof vertically.** That's not what they look like on the map. I went in and out of the house several times, standing on chairs, taking pictures, and showing my dad. *Dad! They are not horizontal!*

📸 **[PHOTO: the panels on the roof]** · 📸 **[SCREENSHOT: the panel map in the app]**

It took some convincing from a difficult angle, but I proved it. And it wasn't just the orientation. The official app (and mine, since it uses the same layout) shows two long rows and then a short row. What's actually on the roof is **long, short, long**. A bona fide discrepancy.

Here's why. Two to three years ago, storms ripped through the neighborhood and damaged our roof. Insurance covered it, but to fix a roof you have to take the solar panels down. The whole process took 18 months. When the panels went back up, everything *seemed* fine. Shortly after, the two microinverters stopped responding.

I'd been blaming the underperformers on wildfire smoke, a dust storm, and bird poop. Then it clicked: whoever reinstalled the panels never updated the map. **The system reports panels in places they are not.** To test it, I checked where a tree's shade actually lands. It does cover some panels. Just not the ones the map says are underperforming.

Why does this matter? If I point a technician at "the second panel in the first row" and it's really the one next to it, he "fixes" the wrong panel, says "you'll see it working tomorrow," and I can't prove anything. That could get expensive. Before I start directing people, I need to know exactly which panel is which. That call to the solar company is coming, and it's going to be a serious one.

### So, was it me?

📸 **[SCREENSHOT: Home use & grid card]**

Partly in my defense: ComEd raised prices about 12% for all residents. Add two dead microinverters (plus whatever is going on with the mystery panels) and a full house, and the bill makes a lot more sense. To be fair, the dashboard also says the house really is using more power than last year, which is exactly why the smart plugs are next. Soon we'll know *who*.

**[YOUR DAD'S REACTION: what did he say when he saw it?]**

## Demo

📸 **[SCREENSHOTS / SHORT VIDEO: dashboard, Problems list, panel map, Dad's briefing]**

The live dashboard is password-protected because it shows our home's real data. **[Add a demo login or video here so judges can see it.]**

## Code

[github.com/AnnaVi11arrea1/solar-dashboard](https://github.com/AnnaVi11arrea1/solar-dashboard)

**[Make the repo public before publishing. You can then swap this link for DEV's GitHub embed tag.]**

## How I Built It

```
Home PC ── collector (Node, every 60 s)
   ├─ Enphase IQ Gateway (local API, per-panel data)
   ├─ Home Assistant (smart plug wattage + rooms)
   └─ Ollama + Gemma 3 4B ── Dad's briefing every 6 h
        │
        ▼
Vercel (Next.js 16) ── Upstash Redis ── dashboard
        ▲
        └─ daily cron → Enphase cloud API (history)
```

- **Next.js 16 on Vercel** for the dashboard, with **Upstash Redis** for storage
- **A small Node collector on our home PC** that reads the Enphase gateway on the local network and Home Assistant every minute
- **Enphase's cloud API** (the free developer tier) for years of history, **ComEd's Green Button export** for the bills, and **PVWatts** for expected production

**The open-source AI piece is Gemma 3 4B running in Ollama on that same home PC.** A dashboard full of charts is great for me, but my dad doesn't want charts. He wants to know three things: is the solar working, why is the bill what it is, and does he need to do anything?

Every six hours the collector asks the dashboard for a small set of facts (today's production versus expected, the latest bill versus last year, the Problems list), hands them to Gemma with instructions to explain them like a helpful family member, and posts the result back to the top of the dashboard. It takes about 20 seconds. Here's a real one:

> Overall, your solar panels produced a good amount of electricity this month.
> - The microinverters 202015011110 and 202101033131 are not reporting. You need to contact Enphase support immediately with the serial numbers to get these fixed under warranty.
> - Your electric bill is $270.48, which is much higher than last year's $46.12. This is because your home uses 76 kWh per day, compared to 44 kWh per day last year.
> - Solar panels covered 41% of your electricity use.

📸 **[SCREENSHOT: Dad's briefing card]**

Building the briefing turned up a bug, too. After sunset, the dashboard told us **0 of 23 panels were working**, with 21 critical alerts. Microinverters run on the panels' own power, so after dark every one of them goes quiet, and the gateway's flags can't tell a dead unit from nightfall. If Gemma had read that, it would have told my dad his whole roof had died. Now a panel only counts as dead after a full day with no report.

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

- **The data stays home.** The briefing is built from our electric bills, our usage, and the details of our system. With a local model, none of that goes to an AI company. It never leaves the PC in our house.
- **It costs nothing to run.** A note every six hours, forever, for $0. A paid API would turn a family tool into a monthly bill, which is a little ironic for an app about lowering the bill.
- **I can swap the model with one line.** It's `OLLAMA_MODEL=gemma3:4b` in a config file. If a better small model comes out, or Dad wants it to sound different, I change one setting. No vendor, no migration.
- **Open data made the whole thing possible.** The solar gateway has a local API on our network, PVWatts is free public data, and the utility exports bills in an open format. Being able to combine them is what exposed the panel mix-up in the first place.

## My Agent Session

I built this with Claude Code, and every session is tracked with **Entire**, which links each AI session to the commits it produced.

**[Add a screenshot of `entire why` on the night-time fix and/or an `entire search` result. Optionally, embed a DevRelay session.]**

## Prize Categories

- **Best Use of Entire**: every AI session in this build is saved and linked to its commits. I can run `entire why` on any line to see the prompt, session, and commit that produced it, and `entire search` across the whole build process. For example, `entire why lib/problems.ts:34` traces the night-time "every panel is dead" fix straight back to the session where we found it.
- **Best Use of Gemma**: Gemma 3 4B, running locally, is what turns the dashboard into something my dad can actually read.

- **Dad's briefing**: a short, plain-English note at the top of the dashboard, written by **Gemma running locally on our home PC**, that explains all of the above without a single chart

I'll be honest, it turned into chaos.

📸 **[SCREENSHOT: full dashboard]**

### The roof mystery

Everything was fun and games at first, connecting an API here, pulling in a spreadsheet there. Our solar company even has a free developer portal. Then I started digging deeper than I'd planned. I learned there was an optional consumption meter our system could have had, but it was never installed. I learned you can put devices on your circuit breaker to see which circuit (or room, like my brother's... *cough cough*) is using what at any moment.

We already knew two of the microinverters were bad. What alarmed me was when my app started warning that some *random* panels were underperforming: four more, reporting between 11% and 30% of their normal output. They weren't clustered in one area.

Confused, I stepped outside to see if a squirrel had built a house up there. Nope, just neatly positioned solar panels... wait. **They run up the roof vertically.** That's not what they look like on the map. I went in and out of the house several times, standing on chairs, taking pictures, and showing my dad. *Dad! They are not horizontal!*

📸 **[PHOTO: the panels on the roof]** · 📸 **[SCREENSHOT: the panel map in the app]**

It took some convincing from a difficult angle, but I proved it. And it wasn't just the orientation. The official app (and mine, since it uses the same layout) shows two long rows and then a short row. What's actually on the roof is **long, short, long**. A bona fide discrepancy.

Here's why. Two to three years ago, storms ripped through the neighborhood and damaged our roof. Insurance covered it, but to fix a roof you have to take the solar panels down. The whole process took 18 months. When the panels went back up, everything *seemed* fine. Shortly after, the two microinverters stopped responding.

I'd been blaming the underperformers on wildfire smoke, a dust storm, and bird poop. Then it clicked: whoever reinstalled the panels never updated the map. **The system reports panels in places they are not.** To test it, I checked where a tree's shade actually lands. It does cover some panels. Just not the ones the map says are underperforming.

Why does this matter? If I point a technician at "the second panel in the first row" and it's really the one next to it, he "fixes" the wrong panel, says "you'll see it working tomorrow," and I can't prove anything. That could get expensive. Before I start directing people, I need to know exactly which panel is which. That call to the solar company is coming, and it's going to be a serious one.

### So, was it me?

📸 **[SCREENSHOT: Home use & grid card]**

Partly in my defense: ComEd raised prices about 12% for all residents. Add two dead microinverters (plus whatever is going on with the mystery panels) and a full house, and the bill makes a lot more sense. To be fair, the dashboard also says the house really is using more power than last year, which is exactly why the smart plugs are next. Soon we'll know *who*.

**[YOUR DAD'S REACTION: what did he say when he saw it?]**

## Demo

📸 **[SCREENSHOTS / SHORT VIDEO: dashboard, Problems list, panel map, Dad's briefing]**

The live dashboard is password-protected because it shows our home's real data. **[Add a demo login or video here so judges can see it.]**

## Code

[github.com/AnnaVi11arrea1/solar-dashboard](https://github.com/AnnaVi11arrea1/solar-dashboard)

**[Make the repo public before publishing. You can then swap this link for DEV's GitHub embed tag.]**

## How I Built It

```
Home PC ── collector (Node, every 60 s)
   ├─ Enphase IQ Gateway (local API, per-panel data)
   ├─ Home Assistant (smart plug wattage + rooms)
   └─ Ollama + Gemma 3 4B ── Dad's briefing every 6 h
        │
        ▼
Vercel (Next.js 16) ── Upstash Redis ── dashboard
        ▲
        └─ daily cron → Enphase cloud API (history)
```

- **Next.js 16 on Vercel** for the dashboard, with **Upstash Redis** for storage
- **A small Node collector on our home PC** that reads the Enphase gateway on the local network and Home Assistant every minute
- **Enphase's cloud API** (the free developer tier) for years of history, **ComEd's Green Button export** for the bills, and **PVWatts** for expected production

**The open-source AI piece is Gemma 3 4B running in Ollama on that same home PC.** A dashboard full of charts is great for me, but my dad doesn't want charts. He wants to know three things: is the solar working, why is the bill what it is, and does he need to do anything?

Every six hours the collector asks the dashboard for a small set of facts (today's production versus expected, the latest bill versus last year, the Problems list), hands them to Gemma with instructions to explain them like a helpful family member, and posts the result back to the top of the dashboard. It takes about 20 seconds. Here's a real one:

> Overall, your solar panels produced a good amount of electricity this month.
> - The microinverters 202015011110 and 202101033131 are not reporting. You need to contact Enphase support immediately with the serial numbers to get these fixed under warranty.
> - Your electric bill is $270.48, which is much higher than last year's $46.12. This is because your home uses 76 kWh per day, compared to 44 kWh per day last year.
> - Solar panels covered 41% of your electricity use.

📸 **[SCREENSHOT: Dad's briefing card]**

Building the briefing turned up a bug, too. After sunset, the dashboard told us **0 of 23 panels were working**, with 21 critical alerts. Microinverters run on the panels' own power, so after dark every one of them goes quiet, and the gateway's flags can't tell a dead unit from nightfall. If Gemma had read that, it would have told my dad his whole roof had died. Now a panel only counts as dead after a full day with no report.

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

- **The data stays home.** The briefing is built from our electric bills, our usage, and the details of our system. With a local model, none of that goes to an AI company. It never leaves the PC in our house.
- **It costs nothing to run.** A note every six hours, forever, for $0. A paid API would turn a family tool into a monthly bill, which is a little ironic for an app about lowering the bill.
- **I can swap the model with one line.** It's `OLLAMA_MODEL=gemma3:4b` in a config file. If a better small model comes out, or Dad wants it to sound different, I change one setting. No vendor, no migration.
- **Open data made the whole thing possible.** The solar gateway has a local API on our network, PVWatts is free public data, and the utility exports bills in an open format. Being able to combine them is what exposed the panel mix-up in the first place.

## My Agent Session

I built this with Claude Code, and every session is tracked with **Entire**, which links each AI session to the commits it produced.

**[Add a screenshot of `entire why` on the night-time fix and/or an `entire search` result. Optionally, embed a DevRelay session.]**

I can run `entire why` on any line to see the prompt, session, and commit that produced it, and `entire search` across the whole build process. For example, `entire why lib/problems.ts:34` traces the night-time "every panel is dead" fix straight back to the session where we found it.
- **Best Use of Gemma**: Gemma 3 4B, running locally, is what turns the dashboard into something my dad can actually read.

---
title: cookies
description: API Reference for the cookies function.
---

`cookies` is an **async** function that allows you to read the HTTP incoming request cookies in [Server Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components), and read/write outgoing request cookies in [Server Functions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data) or [Route Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route).

```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" switcher
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'

export default async function Page() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies()
  const theme = cookieStore.get('theme')
  return '...'
}
```

```js filename="app/page.js" switcher
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'

export default async function Page() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies()
  const theme = cookieStore.get('theme')
  return '...'
}
```

## Reference

### Methods

The following methods are available:

| Method                      | Return Type      | Description                                                                     |
| --------------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `get('name')`               | Object           | Accepts a cookie name and returns an object with the name and value.            |
| `getAll()`                  | Array of objects | Returns a list of all the cookies with a matching name.                         |
| `has('name')`               | Boolean          | Accepts a cookie name and returns a boolean based on if the cookie exists.      |
| `set(name, value, options)` | -                | Accepts a cookie name, value, and options and sets the outgoing request cookie. |
| `delete(name)`              | -                | Accepts a cookie name and deletes the cookie.                                   |
| `toString()`                | String           | Returns a string representation of the cookies.                                 |

### Options

When setting a cookie, the following properties from the `options` object are supported:

| Option        | Type                                   | Description                                                                        |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `name`        | String                                 | Specifies the name of the cookie.                                                  |
| `value`       | String                                 | Specifies the value to be stored in the cookie.                                    |
| `expires`     | Date                                   | Defines the exact date when the cookie will expire.                                |
| `maxAge`      | Number                                 | Sets the cookie’s lifespan in seconds.                                             |
| `domain`      | String                                 | Specifies the domain where the cookie is available.                                |
| `path`        | String, default: `'/'`                 | Limits the cookie's scope to a specific path within the domain.                    |
| `secure`      | Boolean                                | Ensures the cookie is sent only over HTTPS connections for added security.         |
| `httpOnly`    | Boolean                                | Restricts the cookie to HTTP requests, preventing client-side access.              |
| `sameSite`    | Boolean, `'lax'`, `'strict'`, `'none'` | Controls the cookie's cross-site request behavior.                                 |
| `priority`    | String (`"low"`, `"medium"`, `"high"`) | Specifies the cookie's priority                                                    |
| `partitioned` | Boolean                                | Indicates whether the cookie is [partitioned](https://github.com/privacycg/CHIPS). |

content.text:
I committed the night view and judge login as `04dd84b`, and Entire linked it to this session. **I haven't pushed yet.** On Vercel, environment variables only take effect on the next deploy, so the password has to be set before I push.

**One step for you, in the Vercel dashboard:**
1. Go to Project **solar-dashboard**, then **Settings**, then **Environment Variables**.
2. Add `JUDGE_PASSWORD` = `Dev_judge$`, set it to **Production**, and save.
3. Tell me "done". I'll push, which deploys the update and uploads your Entire checkpoints. Then I'll test the judge login on the live site.

**What I tested locally:**
- **Judge login:** `Dev_judge$` opens the dashboard with a "Judge view · bill amounts hidden · access ends November 3, 2026" notice at the top.
  - Wrong passwords are rejected.
  - The judge's login cookie expires at the end of Nov 3, Chicago time, and the server also stops accepting the password then.
  - Judges get 401 on the Enphase and API routes, and the reconnect links are hidden from them.
- **Bill amounts hidden from judges:** the Bill tile and column, the costs on chart hover, and the dollar figures in Gemma's briefing and the Problems list. I found no real dollar amounts in the judge's page. The per-device "≈ $/month" estimates are still visible: they're calculated from your electricity rate rather than taken from the bill. Tell me if you want those hidden too.
- **Night banner:** "Solar panels are not used at night" shows at the top when the panels produce under 10 W, which it's doing right now.

**One limit on the night averages: tonight they won't show yet.** The per-panel counter started this afternoon, so today's totals are partial; a first try showed a misleading 0.04 kWh/day per panel. I changed it to only average complete days, meaning days where the first reading came before sunrise. Every day from midnight tonight on counts, so **tomorrow night** the grid will show real averages. Until then, at night it shows today's readings with a note that averages start after the first full day. If you want a screenshot of the night view for your post, it'll look right after tomorrow's sunset.

content.text:
I made the fix and tested it, but **committing and pushing it was blocked** by the permission check, which flagged it as a possible credential leak. It's a fair concern: the change puts a hash of the judge password into a repo you're about to make public. An unsalted SHA-256 of a short password can be cracked, so in practice anyone reading the code could work out `Dev_judge$`.

**How much that matters:** the account is read-only, every bill amount is hidden, the Enphase controls and API routes are blocked, and it stops working on Nov 3. You'll probably be putting the password in your public DEV post anyway. So the risk is small, but it's your decision.

**Option A: ship the hashed version.** It's done and tested locally. To commit and push it yourself:
```
! git add lib/auth.ts README.md
! git commit -m "Judge login: built-in hashed password instead of a Vercel env var"
! git push origin master
```
If the commit hangs on Entire's hidden prompt, press `y` and Enter.

**Option B: keep the password out of the code and fix the Vercel variable instead.** First discard my change with `! git checkout lib/auth.ts README.md`. The env-var version (`04dd84b`) is already deployed. Something on the Vercel side is wrong, and the usual culprits are:
- the variable is saved under **Preview** or **Development** instead of **Production**
- there's a typo in the name `JUDGE_PASSWORD`
- the value has quotes or a trailing space
- there was no **Redeploy** after saving

A screenshot of that settings row (blur the value) would show me which.

Option A is quickest with about 2 hours left. Tell me which you pick, and once it's live I'll test the judge login on the site again.
